content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use landmark-based distance vectors to capture nodes’ positional information for link prediction. It computes a vector for each node in a graph that contains the node's distances to a selected set of landmarks, which is attached to the feature vector of the node to form the input to a graph neural network for embedding learning and link predictions. The paper shows that the distances to landmarks are good approximations of the distances between nodes, and it analyses the approximation ratio for two graph models. A graph clustering and degree-based strategy is further proposed for landmark selection. Experimental results on a few real graph datasets confirm the effectiveness of the proposed techniques.

content.title: Response to reviewer QvGt
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments and suggestions.

**Q-1. Using distance information in graph embedding is not a new idea (e.g., P- GNN (You et al. 2019)), although the techniques to incorporate the distance information are different.**

A-1. Using distance information has been a fundamental approach for graph embeddings, e.g., as in the celebrated theorem on Bourgain’s embedding [1]. Our work can be regarded as one which reinforces the importance of distance information for representing graphs.

Our method differs significantly from P-GNN in both theoretical and methodological aspects. P-GNN focuses on realizing Bourgain’s embedding guided by Linial’s method [2] and performs message computation and aggregation based on distances to random subset of nodes. By contrast, we judiciously select representative nodes (landmarks) in combination with graph clustering and use the associated distances as input attributes to nodes.

Importantly, our method outperforms P-GNN by a significantly large margin. Please refer to Table 1 of the paper.

**Q-2. It is a bit unclear how exactly are the proposed techniques used in real applications. The distance vectors to the landmarks rely on knowing the full graph adjacency matrix. Under such a setting, the links between all graph nodes are known, assuming that the “links” refer to direct edges between nodes. Why is link prediction still needed in such a setting? If the graph adjacency matrix is only partially known, how does the data scarcity impact the model performance? How are the experiments set up exactly?**

A-2. The adjacency matrix is required only during “training” phase, but not during “prediction” phase, similar to typical approaches for link prediction. This is perhaps best explained with examples. Suppose we have a citation graph among a set of authors in year 2022. The model for link prediction, consisting of a node embedding network and the decoder, is trained with the adjacency information available at 2022 (Fig. 1 shows only the node embedding network. The decoder appended to the embedding network is not shown, but is mentioned in Sec. 4.1). The distance vectors are computed only during the training phase based on the full adjacency matrix.

In 2023, the citation graph will potentially change, and suppose we would like to predict the formation of a new link between, say author A and B. The node embeddings of A and B, pre-computed based on the information from 2022, are passed to the decoder which outputs the confidence of link formation. In our experiments with OGB-COLLAB dataset, we used 2017 graph with full information for training, and used 2018 edges for validation and 2019 edges for testing, using the officially recommended splitting of datasets.

A similar approach can be taken for the task of predicting missing links. In this case, some of link information are assumed to be simply unavailable, because the potential number of links can be much greater than the number of nodes. In experiments, a subset of edges are masked out during training, and those edges are used for validation. Indeed, this can be regarded as having incomplete information on graphs as pointed out by the reviewer. Nonetheless, models are trained with the available information on adjacency,  i.e., GNN-based methods (including P-GNN) require the adjacency matrix during training.

In summary, the model can be trained based on the adjacency matrix available at that point, and predicts future or missing links by utilizing pre- computed node embeddings.

**Q-3. Also, the notations in Section 2.1 consider an adjacent matrix with unit edge weight. What if the edge weights are real numbers and not just 0 or 1? Will the proposed techniques still be applicable?**

A-3. The adjacency matrix need not be a 0-1 matrix in our method. A weighted adjacency matrix can be used in the computation with GNNs. The weights do not affect the distance computation and landmark selection which are based on hop-distances. 
**In the revised paper, we removed 0-1 constraint on adjacency matrices in Sec. 2.1.**

In addition, we ran experiments to compare the cases with unweighted and weighted graphs. In our experiments, the only dataset with weights was OGB-COLLAB which represents a collaboration network between authors. An edge weight represents the number of co-authored papers. Our experiments have used binary edges, e.g., converting nonzero edge weights to 1. By applying weighted adjacency matrix, the performance is 52.42 $\pm$ 0.73 on HIT@50 which is slightly worse than 54.47 $\pm$ 0.75 with binary edges. This demonstrates that weight information may not be necessarily helpful in predicting the existence of edges.  

**References**

[1] Jean Bourgain. On lipschitz embedding of finite metric spaces in hilbert space. Israel Journal of Mathematics, 52(1):46–52, 1985.

[2] Nathan Linial et al. The geometry of graphs and some of its algorithmic applications.Combinatorica, 15(2):215–245, 1995.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a methodology to leverage node positional information in GNNs for link prediction tasks. The basic idea is to consider landmark nodes, i.e., representative nodes that are distributed across the network which can be used to construct distance vectors that are used along the node feature vectors. Specifically, high-degree nodes are chosen as landmarks. The paper provides theoretical justifications based on graph generative models about how well distances can be represented using landmarks. To further improve the task of landmark selection in practice, a clustering-based approach is considered, where high-degree nodes are chosen from each cluster. This motivates the design of the CLAN model which first learns feature representations per cluster and then it computes the final node representations using a GNN. The proposed methodology is evaluated on several real-world graphs, and its performance is compared against various baseline models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*Strengths:*
* The proposed formulation for leveraging landmarks to incorporate positional information in GNNs is interesting. 

* The paper provides a theoretical justification about why high-degree nodes chosen as landmarks can preserve the average distances among nodes. Despite the assumptions made by the different network models, the analysis provides theoretical bounds about the quality of the chosen landmark nodes.

*Weaknesses:*
* Despite the interesting analysis, in practice, a heuristic clustering-based methodology is applied to select the landmark nodes. There are several questions that arise here.

  First, are the theoretical bounds still valid in these settings? Selecting high-degree nodes within each cluster could end up selecting a set of nodes that are not necessarily among the top-degree nodes in the graph.

  Second, in my understanding, landmark nodes should correspond to central nodes in the graph. Several studies in network science have indicated that high-degree nodes are not necessarily the most centrally located ones. Besides computational efficiency, what are the benefits of relying on node degrees vs. other centrality criteria (e.g., betweenness centrality)?

* The methodology assumes that the graph will have some clear community structure. Nevertheless, this does not always hold in real-world networks. How strong is this assumption? The algorithm used to extract clusters could somehow control the structure of clusters. But how will the model perform in the absence of well-defined clusters?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written, and the different concepts are clearly presented. At the same time, the paper keeps a good balance between theoretical contributions and empirical evaluation.  Despite the simplicity of the approach, it constitutes an interesting way to further boost the performance of GNNs.

Some further questions follow below:
* In the CLAN model, an MLP is used the encode node features within each community. Nevertheless, the clusters themselves might have some interesting structural properties. Why not use a GNN to compute the cluster-specific embeddings?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I believe it’s an interesting approach that further boosts the performance of GNNs leveraging node positional information. Nevertheless, I still have some concerns about the methodology (mentioned in the ‘Weaknesses’ part) which need further clarification.

content.title: Response to reviewer FTqm part(1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments and suggestions.

**Q-1. First, In practice, a heuristic clustering-based methodology is applied to select the landmark nodes. are the theoretical bounds still valid in these settings? Selecting high-degree nodes within each cluster could end up selecting a set of nodes that are not necessarily among the top-degree nodes in the graph.**

A-1. We will discuss the bound in Eq. (10) which is relevant to this comment. Eq. (10) shows the distance bound in Barabasi-Albert
(BA) networks. Below we summarize the landmark selection process for BA networks as stated in the paper.
* Create a pool of top-$M(N)$ degree nodes where $M(N)=g(N)\cdot K(N)$.
* Randomly select $K(N)$ nodes as landmarks from the pool of $M(N)$ nodes.

As shown in the paper, the bound is asymptotically optimal even when $g(N)$ is slowly increasing in $N$, e.g., $g(N)=\log N$. This is important, because if we want $K(N)$ landmarks, we do NOT need top-$K(N)$ degree nodes. Instead, we can select $K(N)$ landmarks from a larger pool of top-$\{\log N \cdot K(N)\}$ degree nodes. The extra factor $\log N$ leaves us room for improvement (such as clustering) without affecting the asymptotic optimality of the bound. 


Next, we show that the landmarks from CLAN have sufficiently high degrees even with clustering. We show (1) landmarks from CLAN are among top-$\{\log N \cdot K(N)\}$ similar to TOP-POOL; (2) landmarks from CLAN tend to have higher degrees than those from TOP-POOL. Numerical experiments are used, because theoretical analysis involving clustering seems difficult.

Table Q1 shows the comparison of CLAN and TOP-POOL in BA networks. The numbers represent the average rank of the degrees of landmarks. For example, the rank of degrees of landmarks selected by CLAN is top 5.02\% on average when $N=500$. We set $K(N)=\log N$ as in the paper. Results are averaged over 100 repetitions. 

We observe that the degrees of landmarks selected by CLAN are ranked even higher than TOP-POOL. This is perhaps because our clustering algorithm grows clusters in an iterative and balanced manner, and each cluster quickly picks big "hubs" in BA networks. In addition, in all experiments, the landmarks from CLAN were always within top-$\{\log N \cdot K(N)\}$ degree nodes.

**<Table Q1>**
|Network size $N$|CLAN|TOP-POOL|Fraction of CLAN landmarks in top-{$\log N \cdot K(N)$}|
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|500|5.02\%|6.38\%|100\%|
|1000|3.02\%|4.37\%|100\%|
|5000|1.76\%|2.85\%|100\%|
|10000|0.90\%|1.48\%|100\%||

SUMMARY: The landmarks selected from clustering have sufficiently high degrees in BA networks, and meet the condition on degree distribution for asymptotic optimality of the bound.

**Q-2. Second, in my understanding, landmark nodes should correspond to central nodes in the graph. Several studies in network science have indicated that high-degree nodes are not necessarily the most centrally located ones. Besides computational efficiency, what are the benefits of relying on node degrees vs. other centrality criteria (e.g., betweenness centrality)**

A-2. This is a good point, and we indeed have tried Betweenness and Closeness centralities for landmark selection. Table Q2 shows the experimental results comparing Degree, Betweenness and Closeness centralities. The results show that performances are similar among the centralities. Thus, all the centralities are effective measures for identifying "important" nodes. Degree centrality, however, was slightly better than the other choices. 

More importantly, Betweenness and Closeness centralities require full information on inter-node distances, which incurs high computational overhead. In Table Q2, we excluded datasets CITATION2 and COLLAB which are too large graphs to compute Betweenness and Closeness centralities. Scalability is crucial for link prediction methods. Besides, Degree centrality is consistent with our theoretical derivation. In conclusion, from the perspective of scalability and performance, Degree centrality is the best choice.


**ACTION: We have added the discussion and experiment results on centralities in the Appendix. Please refer to Appendix E: Node Centrality.**

**<Table Q2>**
|Centrality|DDI|PubMed|Cora|Citeseer|Facebook|
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|Degree|**67.02 $\pm$ 6.85**|**96.62 $\pm$ 0.21**|**93.25 $\pm$ 0.15**|**94.75 $\pm$ 0.13**|**99.53 $\pm$ 0.00**|
|Betweeness|66.41 $\pm$ 6.77|96.36 $\pm$ 0.19|92.69 $\pm$ 0.12|94.44 $\pm$ 0.08|99.32 $\pm$ 0.00|
|Closeness|65.56 $\pm$ 6.65|95.92 $\pm$ 0.20|92.43 $\pm$ 0.10|94.65 $\pm$ 0.12|99.35 $\pm$ 0.00|

content.title: Response to reviewer FTqm part(2/2)
content.comment:
**Q-3. The methodology assumes that the graph will have some clear community structure. Nevertheless, this does not always hold in real-world networks. How strong is this assumption? The algorithm used to extract clusters could somehow control the structure of clusters. But how will the model perform in the absence of well-defined clusters?**

A-3. Graphs do not need to have clear community structure for our method to work. Even without clear community structures, our method will partition the network using the clustering algorithm (FluidC). Due to the balancing properties of FluidC as explained in Sec. 3.1, the network will be partitioned into roughly equal-sized clusters. Landmarks will be evenly distributed over the network.

We argue that, such an even distribution of landmarks can prevent the following bad scenario. Suppose a large region of the network does not have landmarks. The landmarks are located far away from the nodes within the area. Thus the landmarks may provide poor estimates on the positional information of nodes. However, it is unlikely that a large region has no landmarks, if the landmarks are evenly distributed over the network. Each landmark will cover roughly equal part of the network. Thus the landmarks can provide a consistent view on the positional information of nodes. 

To support our argument, we evaluated the "modularity" [1] of graph datasets after applying CLAN. For a given graph and its clusters, the modularity score represent the strength of community formation in the clusters. We observe that DDI dataset has the lowest modularity score. However, CLAN achieves the state-of-the-art performance on DDI: CLAN achieved $67.02\pm 6.85$ whereas the second-best performance was $62.30 \pm 9.12$ as shown in Table 1 of the paper. The result shows that CLAN can perform well without clear community structure.

**<Table Q3>** 
||COLLAB|DDI|PubMed|Cora|Citeseer|Facebook|
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|Modularity|0.72|**0.29**|0.74|0.77|0.73|0.75|



**Q-4. In the CLAN model, an MLP is used the encode node features within each community. Nevertheless, the clusters themselves might have some interesting structural properties. Why not use a GNN to compute the cluster-specific embeddings?**

A-4. We indeed have attempted using GNN for cluster-specific embeddings. Table Q4 compares MLP and GNN as the cluster-specific encoder. In all cases, MLP outperformed GNN. The following is a possible explanation. 

The structural properties of the entire graph can be learned at GNN stage with a full adjacency matrix. Thus, it seems unnecessary to apply GNN to clusters in advance. As a generic encoder, we chose MLP to encode distance vectors and node feature attributes. We believe there exist elaborate methods to improve cluster-specific embedding, which is a topic of future research.  

**<Table Q4>**
|Method|COLLAB|DDI|PubMed|Cora|Citeseer|Facebook|
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|MLP|**54.47 $\pm$ 0.75**|**67.02 $\pm$ 6.85**|**96.62 $\pm$ 0.21**|**93.25 $\pm$ 0.15**|**94.75 $\pm$ 0.13**|**99.53 $\pm$ 0.00**|
|GNN|42.41 $\pm$ 0.63|52.15 $\pm$ 8.37|95.68 $\pm$ 0.25|91.91 $\pm$ 0.20|93.77 $\pm$ 0.18|98.31 $\pm$ 0.00|

**References**

[1] Newman, Mark EJ. "Modularity and community structure in networks." Proceedings of the national academy of sciences 103.23 (2006): 8577-8582.

content.title: Response to reviewer zsHd
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments and suggestions.

**Q-1. The idea is not novel enough. There are some similar ideas.**

A-1. Please refer to A-3 in response to Q-3 below.

**Q-2. The experiment is not such convincing.**

A-2. Please refer to A-4 in response to Q-4 below.

**Q-3. But the idea is not novel enough. Similar ideas, such as HyperGraph representation learning, cluster based graph learning have been proposed before.**

A-3. 
We discuss two ideas mentioned by the reviewer:

**1. HyperGraph representation learning.** Hypergraphs have no obvious connection to our work. In a plain graph, an edge connects two nodes. If an edge is generalized to join more than two nodes, it is called a hyperedge. Hypergraphs are graphs with hyperedges. One of the representative works on learning hypergraph representation is HyperGraph Neural Networks (HGNN) [1]. HGNN learns to represent data correlations using hypergraphs as follows. Consider a graph with plain edges. A node and its neighbors connected by plain edges are assumed to be connected with a single hyperedge. HGNN generalizes graph convolution operations for processing such hypergraphs. 

The concept of clusters used in our method has little relationship to hyperedges. Graph clustering in our method partitions a given graph based on local community structure. Moreover, distance-based embeddings combined with clustering are not used in the aforementioned works on hypergraphs.

**2. Cluster-based graph learning.** 
To our knowledge, we are the first to propose distance-based embedding method combined with graph clustering. A recent work in major venues related to graph clustering is ClusterSCL [2]. The main idea is the data augmentation based on nodes' cluster distributions in order to boost performance of contrastive learning for node classification.  ClusterSCL does not relate graph clustering with distance or position embedding, thus differs significantly from our method. Moreover, ClusterSCL is designed specifically for node classification, and thus is not applicable to link prediction tasks. 

**Novelty.** In the practical aspect, we provide a simple method for link prediction achieving state-of-the-art performance in many datasets. In the theoretical aspect, we provide a theoretical analysis of landmark-based distances for Erdos-Renyi (ER) and Barabasi-Albert (BA) models. These are fundamental and widely studied models of random graphs. We prove the asymptotic optimality of landmark-based distances under the BA model. We believe that our work makes a novel contribution to the community in both practical and theoretical aspects.

**Q-4. Moreover, the paper lacks sufficient comparison analysis with these methods or experimental comparison.**

A-4. Below we will compare our work with one using hypergraphs as suggested by the reviewer. We consider HGNN [1] mentioned in A-3, which is a representative work on learning representations of hypergraphs. The experimental results are shown in Table Q4. We observe that CLAN outperforms HGNN in all cases.


**<Table Q4>**

 |Method|PubMed|Cora|Citeseer|Facebook|
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|CLAN|**96.62 $\pm$ 0.21**|**93.25 $\pm$ 0.15**|**95.02 $\pm$ 0.13**|**99.53 $\pm$ 0.00**|
|HGNN|92.82 $\pm$ 0.12|88.58 $\pm$ 0.10|52.80 $\pm$ 0.08|87.20 $\pm$ 0.00|



**Q-5. Besides, the experimental results are not clear. In Table 1, P-GNN on DDI only gets nearly 1\%. How is the evaluation? Why is the value such low?**

A-5. Please refer to work [3] published in ICLR 2022. The authors also report that P-GNN does not perform well on DDI achieving performance of 1--2\%: see Table 2 in [3] (link to the paper:  https://openreview.net/forum?id=e95i1IHcWj). According to [3], the positional encoding proposed by P-GNN may potentially suffer from slow convergence, inaccurate prediction, and high complexity. Besides, P-GNN may not scale well in large graphs such as CITATION2 and COLLAB.

**Q-6. The idea is simple and seems effective. But there are some problems, especially in the experiments.**

A-6. Please refer to A-4 and A-5.

**References**

[1] Yifan Feng, Haoxuan You, Zizhao Zhang, Rongrong Ji, and Yue Gao. Hypergraph neural networks. In Proceedings of the AAAI conference on artificial intelligence, volume 33, pp. 3558–3565, 2019.

[2] Wang, Yanling, et al. ClusterSCL: Cluster-Aware Supervised Contrastive Learning on Graphs. Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference (WWW) 2022

[3] Haorui Wang, Haoteng Yin, Muhan Zhang, and Pan Li. Equivariant and stable positional encoding for more powerful graph neural networks. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2022

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose CLAN as a framework for learning positional information of nodes in a graph specific to link prediction applications. The positional information of nodes is crucial for better link prediction and the authors have shown via well known random model of graphs, that such positional information can be encoded by their distances to certain landmarks in the graph (which are typically high degree centrality nodes). Through practical networks, the authors showcase that their choice of landmarks result in accurate representations of internode shortest distances.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
+ Theoretical justification of why high degree centrality is used as for landmark assignment is well appreciated.

+ The paper presents a good background setting for using representation of distances using landmarks and the intuition for selecting proper landmarks that satisfy basic metric requirements like triangle inequality.

+ The notion of 2-factor approximation for detour via landmarks is well structured for both Erdos Renyi Model and Barabasi-Albert Model. As well as the upper threshold for approximating to the shortest path distance via powers of N.

+ The authors have compared their model CLAN w.r.t SOTA GNN models and have shown better performance in terms of top-K retrieval.

+ The experiments are well structured and detailed process for running the baselines and CLAN are explained for reproducibility.

+ CLAN is also well suited for large dense connected graphs as shown via experiments, where other SOTA methods like SEAL fail. 

Weakness

- Some suitable metric comparisons to show case how CLAN performs better than SOTA would have been better if mentioned in the abstract.  

- Since it is a link prediction task, I think the model proposed in https://faculty.mccombs.utexas.edu/deepayan.chakrabarti/mywww/papers/colt10-linkpred.pdf
makes more sense.

- Definition of beta is not clear in the Fronzcaks model as proposed and how that relates to the parameter for Erdos-Renyi Model.

- For Erdos-Renyi Model, the cost upper bound is shown to have a threshold of 1+eps approximation, it would have been better to showcase via experiments on real world networks if the approximation holds true, and if not upto what confidence.

- Related work needs to be improved since most of the related works mentioned are generic GNN/link prediction models and doesn't fall into the motivation of the problem at hand.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is clearly written.

Quality: The theoretical results focus on graph generative models where Pij = h_i h_j/\beta. There are more complex and realistic graph generators e.g., Forest Fire, Kronecker graphs. There is no analysis in connecting their work with such graphs.

Novelty: There are some novelties in the paper (but does not cross the ICLR bar). That being said, I am ok to recommend accept if the technical quality is high.

Reproducibility: I went through the code, it is well written. However, I have a concern about the stopping criteria. I may be wrong here. It seems that the authors have fixed the number of epochs across all methods. Now there are two issues;
(1) the optimal number of epochs is strongly contingent on the learning rate--- how did the authors set them? Using cross validation?
(2) the optimal learning rate in turn depends on the scale of the gradient (unless one normalizes it, which is not the case here) and the scale of the gradient is strongly dependent on the underlying model architecture. 
Therefore, I feel that fixing the number of epochs and the learning rate and then choosing the final model may be suboptimal for all methods. I would suggest that the authors monitor the validation set hits at each epoch and stop if the validation set hits do not improve for long time.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, I think that the paper has significant room for improvement. I am not very convinced about the experiments as I mentioned above. Also, the paper reports OOM for some baselines. Did the authors try with lower batch size?  Also, can the authors report the complexity of the model in terms of the number of parameters?

content.title: Response to reviewer BKzw part(1/4)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments and suggestions.

**Q-1. Some suitable metric comparisons to show case how CLAN performs better than SOTA would have been better if mentioned in the abstract.**

A-1. There are different metrics (HIT@K, MRR, and AUC) due to the variety of datasets we used for benchmarks. Thus, for each baseline method, we measured the relative improvement in the metrics, and averaged them over the datasets. The average improvement ranged from 8.6\% to 35.2\% relative to previous GNN-based methods. We have revised the abstract accordingly. 

**ACTION:** We have added the following paragraph to abstract.

*Experiments demonstrate that CLAN achieves state-of-the-art performances on various datasets in terms of HIT@K, MRR, and AUC. The improvement in those metrics averaged over datasets ranges from 8.6\% to 35.2\% relative to previous GNN-based methods.*

**Q-2. Since it is a link prediction task, I think the model proposed in
https://faculty.mccombs.utexas.edu/deepayan.chakrabarti/mywww/papers/colt10-linkpred.pdf
makes more sense.**

A-2. The paper suggested by the reviewer published in IJCAI 2011 [1] provides theoretical justification of link prediction heuristics based on the (weighted) number of common neighbors, e.g., method by Adamic \& Adar (AA) [2]. The key assumption is that nodes which are located close in the latent metric space are likely to have a link. The authors prove that the bounds on node distances in latent space becomes tight, if the number of common neighbors or short paths between the nodes  is high.

While the paper provides theoretical insights on important link prediction heuristics, its focus is quite different from our work. The heuristic functions explained in the paper are manually designed having specific forms. A new line of link prediction methods has been since developed based on graph neural networks (GNN). GNNs can learn a link predictor (i.e., unknown heuristic function) adaptively from graphs. In addition, various structural information such as enclosing subgraphs (SEAL), distance/position information (CLAN and P-GNN), etc., can be incorporated into GNN-based models.

GNN-based methods have demonstrated superior performance over existing link prediction heuristics. Importantly, comparison with the AA heuristic has been included in the experiments; please refer to Table 1 of the paper. We observe that CLAN outperforms  AA [2] by a large margin.

[1] Purnamrita Sarkar, Deepayan Chakrabarti, and Andrew W Moore. Theoretical justification of pop-
ular link prediction heuristics. In Twenty-Second International Joint Conference on Artificial
Intelligence, 2011.

[2] Lada A Adamic and Eytan Adar. Friends and neighbors on the web. Social networks, 25(3):211–230, 2003.

**ACTION:** In Sec. 5: Related Work, we added the paper suggested by the reviewer and related discussion. Please refer to the second paragraph of Sec. 5.


**Q-3. Definition of beta is not clear in the Fronzcaks model as proposed and how that relates to the parameter for Erdos-Renyi Model.**

A-3. The definition of beta for Erdos-Renyi (ER) model is identical to that from the original paper by Fronzcak [1]. We explain the definition and its relation to parameters as follows. Let $\langle k \rangle$ denote the mean degree in the ER graph. Then $q_{ij}$ which is the probability of an edge between node $i$ and $j$ is given by 

$q_{ij}  = \frac{h_ih_j}{\beta} = \frac{\langle k\rangle}{N}$

Specifically, the probability $q_{ij}$ of connecting nodes $i$ and $j$ can be factorized into node-specific variables $h_i$ and $h_j$ with some scaling parameter $\beta$. By using $h_i=h_j=\langle k\rangle$ and $\beta=\langle k\rangle N$ as stated in the paper, we obtain constant $q_{ij}$ for all $i,j$

Thus, the number of edges for a given node has distribution  Binomial$(n,p)$ where $n=N$, $p=\langle k\rangle/N$ (assume $N$ is large so $N-1\approx N$). It is well known that, as $n\to\infty$ with mean $np=\langle k\rangle$ fixed, binomial distribution becomes Poisson distribution with mean parameter $\langle k\rangle$. The aforementioned setup is consistent with the ER model.

**ACTION:** We added more explanation on the model parameters. Please refer to the first paragraph of Sec. 2.4. 

[1] Agata Fronczak, Piotr Fronczak, and Janusz A Hołyst. Average path length in random networks.
Physical Review E, 70(5):056110, 2004.

content.title: Response to reviewer BKzw part(2/4)
content.comment:
**Q-4. For Erdos-Renyi Model, the cost upper bound is shown to have a threshold of 1+eps approximation, it would have been better to showcase via experiments on real world networks if the approximation holds true, and if not upto what confidence.**

A-4. Thank you for the interesting suggestion. Below we provide experimental results for real-world networks. Table Q-4 shows the average path length via randomly selected landmarks measured from benchmark datasets. The number of landmarks is set to $N^{1-\epsilon}$ with $\epsilon=0.3, 0.5$ and $0.8$.

Interestingly, the average path length indeed does not exceed $(1+\epsilon)$-factor of the actual distance in all cases. Our interpretation is that, the factor of $(1+\epsilon)$ for ER graphs may serve as a conservative bound for real-world graphs. In ER networks, every node has a similar degree, and thus it is unlikely to choose landmarks that provide short paths like hubs. By contrast, in real-world graphs, the variance of node degree can be higher. Thus, there are chances that several high-degree nodes are selected as landmarks, which can reduce the detour distances.

**Table Q-4**
|**# of landmarks**|**COLLAB**|**DDI**|**PubMed**|**Cora**|**Citeseer**|**Facebook**|**$1+\epsilon$**|
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|$N^{0.3}$|9.01 (117%)|4.53 (145%)|11.90 (163%)|11.41 (157$)|14.99 (144%)|7.26 (136%)|170%|
|$N^{0.5}(\sqrt{N})$|8.79 (115%)|3.90 (125%)|10.31 (141%)|9.61 (132%)|13.04 (126%)|6.76 (127%)|150%|
|$N^{0.8}$|7.92 (104%)|3.44 (110%)|8.31 (114%)|8.03 (110%)|10.93 (105%)|5.77 (108%)|120%|
|actual distances|7.64 (100%)|3.12 (100%)|7.29 (100%)|7.27 (100%)|10.38 (100%)|5.32 (100%)|100%|

**ACTION:** We added the above discussion and results to the appendix. Please refer to Appendix F.

**Q-5. Related work needs to be improved since most of the related works mentioned are generic GNN/link prediction models and doesn't fall into the motivation of the problem at hand.**

A-5. Overall, related work is strengthened in two parts.

1. A new paragraph is added to Sec. 5: Related Work. The paragraph is dedicated to GNN models based on distance and position information. We describe recent models and explain the differences from our method.

2. In the paragraph entitled “Link Prediction”, we added papers related to the link prediction heuristics and analysis which were suggested in Q-2. This was explained in A-2.

**ACTION:** We added a new paragraph specifically covering distance and position-based models in related work. Please refer to the 3rd paragraph entitled *"Distance and Position based GNN models"* of Sec. 5: Related Work. 

**Q-6. The theoretical results focus on graph generative models where $P_{ij} = h_i h_j/\beta$. There are more complex and realistic graph generators, e.g., Forest Fire, Kronecker graphs. There is no analysis in connecting their work with such graphs.**

A-6. Below we provide two reasons behind our approach:

**1. Difficulty of Analysis.** The probability of connection in the expression $P_{ij} = h_i h_j/\beta$ can be factorized into node-specific value terms $h_i$ and $h_j$. Without such properties amenable to analysis, e.g., factorization, the analysis of path lengths in random graphs tend to be quite difficult. The models mentioned by the reviewer, e.g., Forest Fire and Kronecker graphs, are complex models. To our knowledge, the path length analysis does not exist, let alone analysis involving landmarks. Moreover, in the last paragraph of Sec. 4.2.1 of Forest Fire paper [1], the authors explicitly state "Rigorous analysis of the Forest Fire Model appears to be quite difficult." 

**2. Insights from Models.** Even though Forest Fire and Kronecker graphs are intricate models, real world graphs are far more complex. Thus, it is important that models provide useful insights irrespective of its complexity. Despite being simple, ER and BA graphs are fundamental and widely studied models. Moreover, they serve our purpose by representing two extreme cases of degree distributions. ER models generate nodes which are homogeneous in the degree without hubs; BA models generate big hubs, exhibiting scale-free property, power-law degree distribution, and small world phenomena. We provide analysis for both cases, and glean design insights from the analysis, which we believe is a nontrivial contribution to the community.

[1] Leskovec, Jure, Jon Kleinberg, and Christos Faloutsos. "Graph evolution: Densification and shrinking diameters." ACM transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data (TKDD) 1.1 (2007): 2-es.

content.title: Response to reviewer BKzw part(3/4)
content.comment:
**Q-7. It seems that the authors have fixed the number of epochs across all methods. Now there are two issues; (1) the optimal number of epochs is strongly contingent on the learning rate how did the authors set them? Using cross validation? (2) the optimal learning rate in turn depends on the scale of the gradient (unless one normalizes it, which is not the case here) and the scale of the gradient is strongly dependent on the underlying model architecture. Therefore, I feel that fixing the number of epochs and the learning rate and then choosing the final model may be suboptimal for all methods. I would suggest that the authors monitor the validation set hits at each epoch and stop if the validation set hits do not improve for long time.**

A-7. The models in our experiments are *not* trained for the same number of epochs. The number in the code shows the maximum number of epochs, which was set to be sufficiently large. In all models, validation score stalled or decreased after some epochs. After running the training loop for the maximum number of epochs, we picked the model checkpoint saved at the epoch with the best validation score (of course, the result reported in the paper is the performance on *test* set, not the validation set). 

Another reason behind our implementation is that, we used the official training code released by OGB. The official code did not use early stopping, and we used the code with minimal changes. We however agree with the reviewer that early stopping can be an effective technique. Our results would be similar to those with early stopping, because for every model, validation score stalled or worsened before reaching the maximum number of epochs. In the future release of our code, we will add an option of  early stopping.

**Q-8. I am not very convinced about the experiments as I mentioned above.**

A-8. Please refer to A-7.

**Q-9. Also, the paper reports OOM for some baselines. Did the authors try with lower batch size?**

A-9. Please refer to papers in ICML 2022 [1] and ICLR 2022 [2], which also reported OOM results for those baseline. Please note that we respect our peer's work, and paid much attention to a fair comparison. 

In training GNNs (for all models including ours), the entire node features and adjacency matrices are processed at GNN layers. This is the most memory-intensive step, and OOM in baselines occurred mostly at this step. Besides, the batch size typically refers to the mini-batch size of links (pairs of node embeddings) fetched for loss computation and parameter updates. For the aforementioned baselines, decreasing the batch size did not prevent OOM.

[1] Tong Zhao, Gang Liu, Daheng Wang, Wenhao Yu, and Meng Jiang. Learning from counterfactual
links for link prediction. Proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Machine
Learning, volume 162 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, pp. 26911–26926. PMLR,
17–23 Jul 2022

[2] Haorui Wang, Haoteng Yin, Muhan Zhang, and Pan Li. Equivariant and stable positional encoding
for more powerful graph neural networks. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2022

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
We sincerely appreciate the time and effort put by the reviewers.

In particular, we thank the reviewers for encouraging comments including:

* **Theoretical insights:**

-"The paper keeps a good balance between theoretical contributions and empirical evaluation."

-"The paper presents a good background setting for using representation of distances using landmarks and the intuition for selecting proper landmarks"

-"Theoretical justification of why high degree centrality is used as for landmark assignment is well appreciated."

* **Good empirical results supporting theory:**

-"The proposed techniques are shown to outperform recent baselines on multiple real graph datasets."

-"CLAN is also well suited for large dense connected graphs as shown via experiments, where other SOTA methods like SEAL fail."

-"This idea is simple and effective."

* **Reproducibility:**

-"The experiments are well structured and detailed process for running the baselines and CLAN are explained for reproducibility."

-"Source code of the proposed techniques is available."

-"This topic is interesting and this paper is easy to follow."

---
We provided responses to all of the reviewers' comments. For detailed responses, please check the individual comment section.  Below we summarize responses to some common concerns raised by reviewers:

**Validity of experiments.** Reviewer 1 (BKzw) and 2 (zsHd) questioned experimental results showing poor performance and OOM (out-of-memory) for some baseline schemes. However, we cite and point to other recent works which obtained similar results for those baselines.

**Novelty.** Reviewers 1 (BKzw), 2 (zsHd), and 4 (QVGt) asked if CLAN is similar to some of previous methods. CLAN differs significantly from existing link prediction heuristics, hypergraph neural networks, or previous distance-based GNNs. To our knowledge, our work is the first to propose landmark-based representation of distance information combined with graph clustering; and is the first to analyze path lengths via landmarks for Erdos-Renyi and Barabasi-Albert models.

**Applicability of theoretical analysis.** Reviewers 1 (BKzw) and 3 (FTqm) asked if our theoretical results hold for real-world graphs, or with graph clustering. We empirically showed that $(1+\epsilon)$-bound on the distances via landmarks holds for real-world benchmark graphs. We also showed by simulating BA networks, the landmarks selected with graph clustering meet the requirement on degree distribution for the distance bound.

---

Finally, we summarize the changes made in the revised paper.

* **Abstract.**

Reviewer 1 (BKzw) suggested adding a metric comparison of performance gain. We added the comparison to **the last paragraph of the abstract.**

* **Related work.**

Reviewer 1 (BKzw) asked for improving related work. We substantially revised the section; we added a new paragraph entitled **"Distance and Position based GNN models"** dedicated to comparison with existing position and distance-based models. Also, we emphasized the difference and novelty of CLAN compared to those models. In addition, we cited and explained works on link prediction heuristics and their theoretical justification suggested by reviewer 1 (BKzw).

* **Analysis of Random Graph Models.**

Reviewers 1 (BKzw) asked for clarification of definition of $\beta$ and its relation to parameters of ER model. We provided more detailed explanation in **the first paragraph of Sec. 2.4**.

* **Appendix.**

-**APPENDIX E.** Per reviewer 3's (zsHd) suggestion, we performed experiments with different types of node centrality. We added and compared the results with betweenness, closeness and degree centrality, and showed that the degree centrality is the best in both performance and simplicity.

-**APPENDIX F.** Reviewer 1 (BKzw) made an interesting suggestion to check if (1+$\epsilon$) approximation is still valid on real-world networks. We added the experimental results showing that the bound holds for benchmark graph datasets.

-**APPENDIX G.** Per reviewer 1's (BKzw)'s request, we added the comparison of the number of parameters among the models.

Thank you again for the valuable comments for improving our work, and we look forward to the discussion on rebuttals.
